claim: The gene most highly correlated with CDK4 in the Cancer Dependency Map is its coactivator CCND1/Cyclin D1.
source: The gene most highly correlated with CDK4 is its coactivator CCND1/Cyclin D1, demonstrating that relevant genetic relationships in the CDK-RB network are correlated (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: Based on Cancer Dependency Map data analysis showing correlation between CDK4 and CCND1 fitness scores across cell lines

claim: CCNF is the ninth most highly correlated gene with CDK4 in the Cancer Dependency Map.
source: Interestingly, the ninth most highly correlated gene with CDK4 was CCNF, which encodes cyclin F (Bai et al., 1994; Bassermann et al., 2014).
evidence: Based on Cancer Dependency Map data analysis showing correlation between CDK4 and CCNF fitness scores

claim: CCNF is among the top 1% of highly correlated genes when analyzing CDK4, CDK6, CCND1, and RBL1 in the Cancer Dependency Map.
source: CCNF is among the top 1% of highly correlated genes when analyzing several other members of the CDK-RB network, including CDK4, CDK6, CCND1, and RBL1 (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: Based on Cancer Dependency Map data analysis showing correlation between CCNF and multiple CDK-RB network members

claim: CDK4, CDK6, CCND1/Cyclin D1, RBL1, and RBL2 are among the top 85 genes (top 0.5%) most highly correlated with CCNF knockout.
source: Accordingly, when we determined those genes most highly correlated with CCNF knockout, CDK4, CDK6, CCND1/Cyclin D1, RBL1, and RBL2 are among the top 85 genes, out of more than 17,630 (~0.5%; Figure 1A).
evidence: Based on Cancer Dependency Map data analysis showing correlation between CCNF and CDK-RB network genes

claim: Filtering the top CCNF correlated genes by the GO term 'cell division' revealed three sub-networks: the Nde1-kinetochore complex, the Anaphase Promoting Complex/Cyclosome (APC/C), and the CDK-RB network.
source: When we filtered the top CCNF correlated genes by the GO term 'cell division' (Figure 1C), three sub-networks emerged: the Nde1-kinetochore complex, the Anaphase Promoting Complex/Cyclosome (APC/C), and the CDK-RB network.
evidence: Based on Gene Ontology filtering of Cancer Dependency Map data

claim: E2F7 and FZR1 are known cyclin F substrates identified among the top CCNF correlated genes.
source: Among the remaining genes/proteins were two known cyclin F substrates: E2F7, which encodes the transcriptional repressor E2F7 (Yuan et al., 2019), and FZR1, which encodes the APC/C coactivator protein, Cdh1 (Choudhury et al., 2016).
evidence: Based on prior published studies identifying E2F7 and FZR1 as cyclin F substrates

claim: Cyclin F overexpression causes a specific downregulation of endogenous p130 in MCF-7 and T47D breast cancer cell lines, whereas CDK4, CDK6, cyclin D1, and p107 remain unchanged.
source: We observed a specific downregulation of endogenous p130 in both cell lines, whereas all other proteins remained unchanged (Figure 1D).
evidence: Based on immunoblot analysis of MCF-7 and T47D cells with doxycycline-inducible cyclin F expression

claim: p130 levels decrease in a time-dependent manner following cyclin F induction, and this can be prevented by inhibiting the proteasome with MG132 or cullin RING E3 ligases using the neddylation inhibitor MLN4924.
source: Similarly, p130 levels decrease in a time-dependent manner following doxycycline treatment, and this can be prevented by inhibiting the proteasome with MG132, or cullin RING E3 ligases, using the neddylation inhibitor MLN4924 (Figure 1—figure supplement 3B; Ohh et al., 2002; Soucy et al., 2009).
evidence: Based on immunoblot analysis of T47D cells with cyclin F induction and proteasome/neddylation inhibitors

claim: Cyclin F protein levels significantly decrease in quiescence, whereas p130 protein levels increase, establishing an inverse expression pattern in human fibroblasts.
source: In each of cell lines tested (BJ, IMR-90, and NHF-1), cyclin F protein levels significantly decrease in quiescence, whereas p130 protein levels increase, establishing an inverse expression pattern (Figure 1E).
evidence: Based on immunoblot analysis comparing asynchronous and quiescent human fibroblasts

claim: Cyclin F protein begins to accumulate as cells re-enter the cell cycle at G1/S after release from quiescence.
source: Cyclin F protein began to accumulate as cells re-entered the cell cycle at G1/S, similar to what was previously reported (Choudhury et al., 2017; D'Angiolella et al., 2012; Figure 1—figure supplement 3C).
evidence: Based on immunoblot analysis of NHF-1 cells released from quiescence and prior published studies

claim: p130 is degraded as cells exit quiescence.
source: Meanwhile, p130 was degraded as cells exited quiescence.
evidence: Based on immunoblot analysis of NHF-1 cells released from quiescence

claim: In cells treated with MLN4924, neither p130 nor p27 is degraded upon release from quiescence.
source: In cells treated with MLN4924, neither p130 nor p27 is degraded, cyclin E accumulates but does not get degraded, and there is a significant delay in cyclin A accumulation (Figure 1F and Figure 1—figure supplement 3D).
evidence: Based on immunoblot analysis of NHF-1 and T98G cells released from quiescence with MLN4924 treatment

claim: p130 protein levels are higher in CCNF knockout HeLa cells compared to control cells.
source: In HeLa cells, p130 protein levels are higher in CCNF KO cells (sgCCNF) than in control cells (sgCTRL; Figure 2A).
evidence: Based on immunoblot analysis of CCNF knockout and control HeLa cells

claim: p130 levels are higher in CCNF knockout HeLa cells at every time point after release from G1/S synchronization compared to control cells.
source: Next, CCNF KO and control HeLa cells were synchronized at G1/S by double thymidine block. After release, p130 levels were higher in the CCNF knockouts at every time point analyzed (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Based on immunoblot analysis of synchronized CCNF knockout and control HeLa cells

claim: Cyclin F depletion increases p130 levels in NHF-1 and IMR-90 cells with two different siRNAs.
source: We then transiently depleted cyclin F from NHF-1 or IMR-90 cells. Cyclin F depletion increased p130 in both cell lines and with two different siRNAs (Figure 2B).
evidence: Based on immunoblot analysis of NHF-1 and IMR-90 cells transfected with siRNAs targeting CCNF

claim: CCNF knockout HeLa cells do not exhibit significant defects in overall cell cycle compared to control cells.
source: Neither CCNF KO HeLa cells, nor the transiently depleted NHF-1 or IMR-90 cells, exhibited significant defects in overall cell cycle compared to their respective controls, judged by propidium iodide staining and analyzed by flow cytometry (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B-D).
evidence: Based on flow cytometry analysis of cell cycle distribution

claim: Endogenous cyclin F co-immunoprecipitates endogenous p130 from HEK293T and U2OS cells.
source: Consistent with the regulation of p130 by cyclin F resulting from a physical interaction, endogenous cyclin F co-immunoprecipitated endogenous p130 from HEK293T and U2OS cells (Figure 2C).
evidence: Based on co-immunoprecipitation experiments in HEK293T and U2OS cells

claim: Increasing amounts of FLAG-cyclin F reduce HA-p130 levels in a dose-dependent manner in HEK293T cells.
source: In HEK293T cells transfected with HA-tagged p130 (HA-p130), increasing amounts of FLAG-tagged cyclin F (FLAG-cyclin F) reduced p130 levels in a dose-dependent manner (Figure 3A).
evidence: Based on immunoblot analysis of HEK293T cells transfected with HA-p130 and increasing amounts of FLAG-cyclin F

claim: p130 levels decrease only upon co-expression with cyclin F and not with Skp2, Fbxw7, βTRCP1, or βTRCP2 in HEK293T and U2OS cells.
source: We therefore transiently expressed HA-p130 alone or together with cyclin F, Skp2, Fbxw7, βTRCP1, or βTRCP2, and in both HEK293T and U2OS cells. p130 levels decreased only upon co-expression with cyclin F and not with any of the other F-box proteins (Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Based on immunoblot analysis of HEK293T and U2OS cells transfected with HA-p130 and various F-box proteins

claim: The reduction in HA-p130 caused by FLAG-cyclin F expression is reversed by addition of MG132 or MLN4924 in HEK293T cells.
source: In HEK293T cells, the reduction in HA-p130 caused by FLAG-cyclin F expression is reversed by addition of MG132 or MLN4924 (Figure 3C).
evidence: Based on immunoblot analysis of HEK293T cells transfected with HA-p130 and FLAG-cyclin F, treated with proteasome or neddylation inhibitors

claim: Cyclin F recognizes its substrates through a hydrophobic patch motif in its cyclin domain (sequence MRYIL at amino acids M309-L313).
source: Cyclin F recognizes its substrates through a hydrophobic patch motif in its cyclin domain (sequence MRYIL at amino acids M309-L313).
evidence: Based on established knowledge about cyclin F substrate recognition

claim: Mutating the methionine and leucine residues to alanine in cyclin F (M309A L313A) can impair cyclin F binding to substrates.
source: Previous studies have shown that mutating the methionine and leucine residues to alanine (Cyclin F M309A L313A) can impair cyclin F binding to substrates (Choudhury et al., 2016; D'Angiolella et al., 2012; D'Angiolella et al., 2010).
evidence: Based on prior published studies showing the effect of cyclin F mutations on substrate binding

claim: Cyclin F (WT) robustly downregulates p130 protein levels, whereas cyclin F (M309A L313A) is unable to promote p130 degradation.
source: Notably, whereas cyclin F (WT) robustly downregulated p130 protein levels, cyclin F (M309A L313A) was unable to promote p130 degradation (Figure 3D).
evidence: Based on immunoblot analysis of HEK293T cells transfected with HA-p130 and wild-type or mutant cyclin F

claim: Cyclin F recognizes Cy Motifs in substrates, which corresponds to the amino acid sequence RxL/I (where x=any amino acid).
source: Cyclin F recognizes Cy Motifs in substrates, which corresponds to the amino acid sequence RxL/I (where x=any amino acid)(Choudhury et al., 2016; D'Angiolella et al., 2012; D'Angiolella et al., 2010).
evidence: Based on prior published studies characterizing cyclin F substrate recognition motifs

claim: There are 13 putative Cy motif sequences in p130 that span the length of the protein.
source: There are 13 putative Cy motif sequences in p130 that span the length of the protein.
evidence: Based on sequence analysis of p130 protein

claim: p130 degradation depends on the presence of a flexible spacer region located between regions A and B in the p130 pocket domain.
source: We transiently expressed each HA-p130 truncation alone, or together with FLAG-cyclin F (WT) and included conditions with and without proteasome and neddylation inhibitors. p130 degradation depended on the presence of a flexible spacer region, located between regions A and B in the p130 pocket domain (Figure 4A, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Based on immunoblot analysis of HEK293T cells transfected with various p130 truncations and cyclin F

claim: Within the p130 spacer region, there are two RxL/I motifs: R658-I660 and R680-L682.
source: Within the spacer, there are two RxL/I motifs: R658-I660 and R680-L682.
evidence: Based on sequence analysis of the p130 spacer region

claim: Only the p130 (R680A L682A) mutant is resistant to cyclin F mediated degradation, demonstrating that these two amino acids alone are required for cyclin F to trigger p130 degradation.
source: We mutated the first and last amino acid in each motif to alanine (AxA) in full-length HA-p130. Only the p130 (R680A L682A) mutant was resistant to cyclin F mediated degradation, demonstrating that these two amino acids alone are required for cyclin F to trigger p130 degradation (Figure 4B).
evidence: Based on immunoblot analysis of HEK293T cells transfected with wild-type or mutant p130 and cyclin F

claim: The p130 sequence at R680-L682 and many surrounding residues are conserved in p130 proteins found in clawed frogs (Xenopus tropicalis), chickens (Gallus gallus), and mice (Mus musculus).
source: That sequence and many surrounding residues are conserved in p130 proteins found in other species, including clawed frogs (Xenopus tropicalis), chickens (Gallus gallus), and mice (Mus musculus) (Figure 4B).
evidence: Based on amino acid sequence alignment of p130 from different species

claim: FLAG-cyclin F binds to GST-p130(WT) but not to GST-p130(AA) or GST alone in GST-pulldown assays.
source: In a GST-pulldown assay, FLAG-cyclin F bound to GST-p130(WT), but not to GST-p130(AA) or GST alone (Figure 4C, left panel).
evidence: Based on GST-pulldown assays using purified GST-p130 and cell lysates containing FLAG-cyclin F

claim: FLAG-cyclin F purified from HEK293T cells precipitates GST-p130(WT) but not GST-p130(AA).
source: Conversely, FLAG-cyclin F, purified from HEK29T cells precipitated GST-p130(WT) but not GST-p130(AA) (Figure 4C, right panel).
evidence: Based on FLAG-pulldown assays using purified FLAG-cyclin F and purified GST-p130

claim: Cyclin F(M309A L313A) cannot bind to GST-p130.
source: Consistent with its inability to trigger p130 degradation, cyclin F(M309A L313A) could not bind to GST-p130 (Figure 4D).
evidence: Based on GST-pulldown and FLAG-pulldown assays using mutant cyclin F and GST-p130

claim: The p130 Cy motif at R680-L682 and the cyclin F hydrophobic patch (M309-L313) are required for the p130-cyclin F interaction and for p130 degradation.
source: Thus, the p130 Cy motif at R680-L682 and the cyclin F hydrophobic patch (M309-L313) are required for the p130-cyclin F interaction and for p130 degradation.
evidence: Based on binding and degradation assays using wild-type and mutant p130 and cyclin F

claim: Recombinant, purified cyclin F25–546-Skp1 dimer binds to TAMRA-labeled p130 peptide (residues 674–692) with a Kd of 0.21±0.01 μM.
source: We titrated recombinant, purified cyclin F25–546-Skp1 dimer into a solution of synthetic, TAMRA-labeled, p130 peptide (residues 674–692) and observed a Kd of 0.21±0.01 μM (Figure 4E, left panel).
evidence: Based on fluorescence polarization anisotropy assays using purified proteins and synthetic peptides

claim: Binding of cyclin F to TAMRA-labeled p130 peptide is efficiently competed away using purified GST-p130(WT) protein but not using GST-p130(AA), which has >50-fold higher Ki in the competition assay.
source: Binding was efficiently competed away using purified GST-p130(WT) protein but not using GST-p130(AA), which had >50-fold higher Ki in the competition assay (Figure 4E, right panel).
evidence: Based on fluorescence polarization anisotropy competition assays using purified proteins

claim: An unlabeled E2F1 peptide containing the relevant Cy motif (residues 84–99) competes with the p130 probe for cyclin F binding.
source: We found that an unlabeled E2F1 peptide containing the relevant Cy motif (residues 84–99), which was previously shown to mediate cyclin F-E2F1 association (Clijsters et al., 2019), also competed with the p130 probe.
evidence: Based on fluorescence polarization anisotropy competition assays and prior published studies

claim: GST-p130(WT) but not GST-p130(AA) can efficiently compete the E2F1 peptide from cyclin F binding.
source: We performed a similar competition assay using a TAMRA labeled E2F184–99 peptide as a probe, and we found that we could efficiently compete the E2F1 peptide with GST-p130(WT) but not GST-p130(AA) (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Based on fluorescence polarization anisotropy competition assays using purified proteins and synthetic peptides

claim: p130 directly binds cyclin F-Skp1 at a site that overlaps with the E2F1 binding site and the association is dependent on critical interactions made by R680 and L682 in p130.
source: We conclude that p130 directly binds cyclin F-Skp1 at a site that overlaps with the E2F1 binding site and that the association is dependent on critical interactions made by R680 and L682 in p130.
evidence: Based on fluorescence polarization anisotropy assays showing direct binding and competition experiments

claim: SCFCyclin F robustly ubiquitinates GST-p130(WT) in vitro.
source: SCFCyclin F robustly ubiquitinated GST-p130(WT) (Figure 5A).
evidence: Based on in vitro ubiquitination assays using purified components

claim: Ubiquitination of p130 by SCFCyclin F is dependent on the inclusion of NEDD8-Cul1-Roc1, Skp1-Cyclin F, and ARIH1/UBCH7.
source: This modification was dependent on the inclusion of NEDD8-Cul1-Roc1, Skp1-Cyclin F, and ARIH1/UBCH7, since the exclusion of any of these components completely abrogated ubiquitination (Figure 5A).
evidence: Based on in vitro ubiquitination assays with and without specific components

claim: GST-p130(AA) is unable to be ubiquitinated by SCFcyclin F.
source: Significantly, GST-p130(AA) was unable to be ubiquitinated by SCFcyclin F.
evidence: Based on in vitro ubiquitination assays using mutant p130

claim: p130(WT) half-life is significantly reduced by ectopic expression of cyclin F in HEK293T cells.
source: While p130(WT) half-life was significantly reduced by ectopic expression of cyclin F, p130(AA) remained stable for the length of the experiment in the presence or absence of cyclin F (Figure 5B–C and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A), indicating that protein levels of p130(AA) are resistant to cyclin F-mediated degradation.
evidence: Based on cycloheximide chase experiments in HEK293T cells

claim: p130(AA) remains stable in the presence or absence of cyclin F in cycloheximide chase experiments.
source: While p130(WT) half-life was significantly reduced by ectopic expression of cyclin F, p130(AA) remained stable for the length of the experiment in the presence or absence of cyclin F (Figure 5B–C and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A), indicating that protein levels of p130(AA) are resistant to cyclin F-mediated degradation.
evidence: Based on cycloheximide chase experiments in HEK293T and U2OS cells

claim: p130(WT) levels are decreased in nocodazole-synchronized cells compared to p130(AA) levels.
source: Interestingly, p130(WT) levels are decreased in nocodazole-synchronized cells compared to p130(AA) levels (Figure 5D).
evidence: Based on immunoblot analysis of synchronized NHF-1 cells expressing inducible p130

claim: Nocodazole synchronization significantly decreases endogenous p130 protein levels in NHF-1 cells.
source: Consistently, nocodazole synchronization significantly decreased endogenous p130 protein levels in NHF-1 cells (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Based on immunoblot analysis of nocodazole-synchronized NHF-1 cells

claim: p130(WT) levels decrease in nocodazole synchronized NHF-1 cells, whereas levels of p130(AA) remain stable.
source: Taken Together, these data indicate that p130(WT) levels decrease in nocodazole synchronized NHF-1 cells, whereas levels of p130(AA) remain stable.
evidence: Based on immunoblot analysis of synchronized NHF-1 cells expressing inducible p130

claim: Similar amounts of cyclin A and E co-purify with HA-p130(WT) and HA-p130(AA) in immunoprecipitation experiments.
source: We immunoprecipitated (IP) HA and found that similar amounts of cyclin A and E co-purify with HA-p130(WT) and HA-p130(AA) (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: Based on co-immunoprecipitation experiments in NHF-1 cells expressing inducible p130

claim: Both HA-p130(WT) and HA-p130(AA) co-immunoprecipitate with endogenous cyclin A.
source: Reciprocally, following IP of endogenous cyclin A, both HA-p130(WT) and HA-p130(AA) co-immunoprecipitated (Figure 5—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: Based on co-immunoprecipitation experiments in NHF-1 cells expressing inducible p130

claim: HA-tagged p130(WT) and p130(AA) are similarly phosphorylated on the CDK site at S672.
source: Further, we assessed whether mutation of the p130 Cy motif would impair p130 phosphorylation. HA-tagged p130(WT) and p130(AA) immunoprecipitated from NHF-1 cells are similarly phosphorylated on the CDK site at S672 (Figure 5—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: Based on immunoblot analysis of immunoprecipitated p130 from NHF-1 cells

claim: HA-p130(WT) and HA-p130(AA) migrate similarly in SDS-PAGE, and their migration is similarly increased by post-lysis phosphatase treatment with calf intestinal phosphatase (CIP).
source: Additionally, HA-p130(WT) and HA-p130(AA) migrate similarly in SDS-PAGE, their migration was similarly increased by post-lysis phosphatase treatment with calf intestinal phosphatase (CIP), and this could be prevented by the addition of phosphatase inhibitors (Figure 5—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: Based on immunoblot analysis of NHF-1 cell lysates treated with phosphatase

claim: HA-tagged p130(WT) and p130(AA) can associate with the DREAM complex based on the co-IP of Lin54.
source: Further, HA-tagged p130(WT) and p130(AA) can associate with the DREAM complex based on the co-IP of Lin54 following an HA pulldown (Figure 5—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: Based on co-immunoprecipitation experiments in NHF-1 cells expressing inducible p130

claim: The Cy motif mutations in p130 do not impact p130 binding to large T-antigen in HEK293T cells or the E7 oncoprotein in HeLa cells.
source: Finally, we determined that the Cy motif mutations did not impact p130 binding to large T-antigen in HEK293T cells or the E7 oncoprotein in HeLa cells (Figure 5—figure supplement 2E-F).
evidence: Based on co-immunoprecipitation experiments in HEK293T and HeLa cells

claim: Although protein levels of p130(WT) and p130(AA) are initially equal after induction, p130(AA) accumulates to higher levels compared to p130(WT) over time.
source: Although protein levels of p130(WT) and p130(AA) are initially equal, p130(AA) accumulated to higher levels compared to p130(WT) over time (Figure 6A), consistent with p130(AA) being resistant to degradation.
evidence: Based on immunoblot analysis of NHF-1 cells expressing inducible p130 over 14 days

claim: Expression of non-degradable p130(AA) leads to a profound decrease in proliferation/viability based on a PrestoBlue assay.
source: Expression of non-degradable p130(AA) led to a profound decrease in proliferation/viability based on a PrestoBlue assay (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Based on PrestoBlue cell viability assays in NHF-1 cells expressing inducible p130

claim: After 14 days, the PrestoBlue signal is decreased 5.8-fold (~83%) in p130(AA)-expressing cells relative to p130(WT) controls.
source: After 14 days, the PrestoBlue signal was decreased 5.8-fold (~83%) in p130(AA)-expressing cells relative to p130(WT) controls.
evidence: Based on PrestoBlue cell viability assays in NHF-1 cells expressing inducible p130

claim: p130(AA)-expressing cells proliferate much more slowly than p130(WT)-expressing cells.
source: Next, we directly quantified proliferation by counting cells every 48 hr for 2 weeks after p130(WT) or p130(AA) induction. The p130(AA)-expressing cells proliferated much more slowly than the p130(WT)-expressing cells (Figure 6B).
evidence: Based on cell counting experiments in NHF-1 cells expressing inducible p130

claim: After 14 days, there are 7.7-fold (~87%) fewer cells in the p130(AA) population compared to p130(WT)-expressing controls.
source: After 14 days, there were 7.7-fold (~87%) less cells in the p130(AA) population compared to p130(WT)-expressing controls.
evidence: Based on cell counting experiments in NHF-1 cells expressing inducible p130

claim: The average doubling time is 33 hr for p130(WT)-expressing cells and 48 hr for p130(AA)-expressing cells.
source: The average doubling time was 33 hr for p130(WT)-expressing cells and 48 hr for p130(AA)-expressing cells (Figure 6C).
evidence: Based on cell counting experiments in NHF-1 cells expressing inducible p130

claim: There is no difference in proliferation between p130(WT) and p130(AA) cell lines treated with vehicle alone across a 2-week experiment.
source: As a control, both cell lines were treated with vehicle alone. There was no difference in proliferation across a 2-week experiment (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B-C).
evidence: Based on cell counting experiments in NHF-1 cells without p130 induction

claim: Ectopic expression of p130(WT) slows the doubling time compared to cells treated with vehicle, consistent with previous studies which report p130 overexpression slows cell growth.
source: Expectedly, ectopic expression of p130(WT) slowed the doubling time compared to cells treated with vehicle, consistent with previous studies which report p130 overexpression slows cell growth (Lacy and Whyte, 1997).
evidence: Based on cell counting experiments and prior published studies

claim: p130(AA) has a much more severe impact on proliferation/survival than p130(WT).
source: However, p130(AA) had a much more severe impact on proliferation/survival.
evidence: Based on cell counting and viability assays comparing p130(WT) and p130(AA) expressing cells

claim: The percent of p130(AA)-expressing cells in G0/G1 significantly increases at days 5 and 7 compared to p130(WT)-expressing cells.
source: The percent of p130(AA)-expressing cells in G0/G1 significantly increased at days 5 and 7 compared to p130(WT)-expressing cells, while the percentage of S-phase cells was significantly decreased (Figure 6D and Figure 6—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Based on flow cytometry analysis of EdU incorporation and DNA staining in NHF-1 cells expressing inducible p130

claim: The percentage of S-phase cells is significantly decreased in p130(AA)-expressing cells compared to p130(WT)-expressing cells at days 5 and 7.
source: The percent of p130(AA)-expressing cells in G0/G1 significantly increased at days 5 and 7 compared to p130(WT)-expressing cells, while the percentage of S-phase cells was significantly decreased (Figure 6D and Figure 6—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Based on flow cytometry analysis of EdU incorporation and DNA staining in NHF-1 cells expressing inducible p130

claim: Beyond day 10, there is no difference in G0/G1% between p130(AA) and p130(WT)-expressing cells, suggesting that the cell population may adapt to the increased levels of p130.
source: Surprisingly, beyond day 10, there was no difference in G0/G1% between p130(AA) and p130(WT)-expressing cells, suggesting that the cell population may adapt to the increased levels of p130, which remain elevated throughout the entire 2-week experiment (Figure 6D).
evidence: Based on flow cytometry analysis of EdU incorporation and DNA staining in NHF-1 cells expressing inducible p130

claim: RB phosphorylation is decreased in p130(AA)-expressing cells at days 5, 7, and 10 compared to p130(WT)-expressing cells or vehicle-treated controls.
source: RB phosphorylation was decreased in p130(AA)-expressing cells at days 5, 7, and 10 compared to p130(WT)-expressing cells or vehicle-treated controls (Figure 6E).
evidence: Based on iterative immunofluorescence imaging (4i) of NHF-1 cells expressing inducible p130

claim: p21 is increased in p130(AA)-expressing cells at days 5, 7, and 10, consistent with a G0/G1 arrest.
source: We also found that p21 was increased in p130(AA)-expressing cells at days 5, 7, and 10, consistent with a G0/G1 arrest (Figure 6F).
evidence: Based on iterative immunofluorescence imaging (4i) of NHF-1 cells expressing inducible p130

claim: A larger percentage of p130(AA)-expressing cells have <4C DNA content compared to p130(WT)-expressing cells at days 5, 7, and 10, consistent with cells accumulating in G0/G1-phase.
source: DNA content analysis revealed that a larger percentage of p130(AA)-expressing cells had <4C DNA content compared to p130(WT)-expressing cells at days 5, 7, and 10, consistent with cells accumulating in G0/G1-phase (Figure 6—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: Based on iterative immunofluorescence imaging (4i) of NHF-1 cells expressing inducible p130

claim: p130(AA) is more localized to the nucleus at days 5 and 7 compared to p130(WT), consistent with p130(AA) mediating cell cycle arrest through cell cycle gene repression.
source: Finally, we assessed the subcellular localization of p130 at each time point by quantifying the ratio of nuclear:cytoplasmic intensity from immunofluorescence images. We found p130(AA) was more localized to the nucleus at days 5 and 7 compared to p130(WT) (Figure 6G and Figure 6—figure supplement 2B), consistent with p130(AA) mediating cell cycle arrest through cell cycle gene repression.
evidence: Based on iterative immunofluorescence imaging (4i) of NHF-1 cells expressing inducible p130

claim: There is a significant reduction in expression of CCNF, CCNE1, CDC6, DHFR, E2F1, and CDT1 in p130(AA)-expressing cells compared to those expressing p130(WT).
source: There was a significant reduction in expression of all of these in p130(AA)-expressing cells compared to those expressing p130(WT) (Figure 7A).
evidence: Based on RT-qPCR analysis of NHF-1 cells expressing inducible p130

claim: The expression of CCNF, CCNE1, CDC6, DHFR, E2F1, and CDT1 is lower in both p130(WT)- and p130(AA)-expressing cells compared to controls.
source: Since both p130(WT)-expressing cells and p130(AA)-expressing cells grew more slowly than cells not expressing a p130 transgene, we also performed RT-qPCR on control cells; the expression of CCNF, CCNE1, CDC6, DHFR, E2F1, and CDT1 was lower in both p130(WT)- and p130 (AA)-expressing cells compared to controls (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Based on RT-qPCR analysis of NHF-1 cells with and without p130 induction

claim: Ectopic expression of p130 reduces transcription of DREAM target genes, which is further decreased by the expression of p130(AA).
source: Thus, ectopic expression of p130 reduces transcription of DREAM target genes, which is further decreased by the expression of p130(AA).
evidence: Based on RT-qPCR analysis of NHF-1 cells expressing inducible p130

claim: Protein levels of CDC6 and Cdt1 are decreased from days 5 to 10 in p130(AA)-expressing cells compared to p130(WT)-expressing cells.
source: Consistent with DREAM activation, as well as observed G0/G1 arrest, protein levels of both CDC6 and Cdt1 were decreased from days 5 to 10 in p130(AA)-expressing cells compared to p130(WT)-expressing cells (Figure 7B–C).
evidence: Based on iterative immunofluorescence imaging (4i) of NHF-1 cells expressing inducible p130

claim: Cleaved PARP is observed in the p130(AA)-expressing population at days 7, 10, and 14, indicating that cells in these populations are undergoing apoptosis.
source: We observe cleaved PARP in the p130(AA)-expressing population at days 7, 10, and 14, and cleaved caspase 3 at days 7 and 10, indicating that cells in these populations are undergoing apoptosis.
evidence: Based on immunoblot analysis of apoptotic markers in NHF-1 cells expressing inducible p130

claim: Cleaved caspase 3 is observed in the p130(AA)-expressing population at days 7 and 10.
source: We observe cleaved PARP in the p130(AA)-expressing population at days 7, 10, and 14, and cleaved caspase 3 at days 7 and 10, indicating that cells in these populations are undergoing apoptosis.
evidence: Based on immunoblot analysis of apoptotic markers in NHF-1 cells expressing inducible p130

claim: Cleaved PARP or cleaved caspase 3 are not observed in p130(WT)-expressing cells.
source: We did not observe cleaved PARP or cleaved caspase in any of the populations for p130(WT)-expressing cells (Figure 7—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: Based on immunoblot analysis of apoptotic markers in NHF-1 cells expressing inducible p130

claim: A higher percentage of apoptotic/necrotic cells is observed in the p130(AA)-expressing population compared to the p130(WT)-expressing population at day 8.
source: Additionally, we performed flow cytometry for Annexin V and propidium iodide incorporation in unfixed cells to assess apoptosis/necrosis. We observed a higher percentage of apoptotic/necrotic cells in the p130(AA)-expressing population compared to the p130(WT)-expressing population at day 8 (Figure 7—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: Based on flow cytometry analysis of Annexin V and propidium iodide staining in NHF-1 cells expressing inducible p130

claim: In p130(AA)-expressing cells at days 5, 7, and 10, levels of 53BP1, phospho-Chk1, and phospho-H2A.X are downregulated.
source: We found that in the p130(AA)-expressing cells at days 5, 7, and 10, that levels of 53BP1, phospho-Chk1, and phospho-H2A.X were downregulated (Figure 7—figure supplement 2C-E).
evidence: Based on iterative immunofluorescence imaging (4i) of NHF-1 cells expressing inducible p130

claim: A decrease in DNA damage markers is consistent with fewer cells being in S-phase and suggests that DNA damage is not the cause of apoptosis in p130(AA)-expressing cells.
source: A decrease in DNA damage markers is consistent with fewer cells being in S-phase and suggests that DNA damage is not the cause of apoptosis.
evidence: Based on iterative immunofluorescence imaging (4i) showing decreased DNA damage markers in p130(AA)-expressing cells

claim: The RB-like protein p130 is a substrate of the E3 ubiquitin ligase SCFCyclin F.
source: We demonstrate that the RB-like protein p130 is a substrate of the E3 ubiquitin ligase SCFCyclin F.
evidence: Based on multiple experiments showing cyclin F binds, ubiquitinates, and regulates p130

claim: Cyclin F loss allows p130 to accumulate.
source: Cyclin F loss allows p130 to accumulate, whereas its overexpression promotes p130 degradation.
evidence: Based on experiments showing increased p130 in CCNF knockout cells and decreased p130 with cyclin F overexpression

claim: Cyclin F overexpression promotes p130 degradation.
source: Cyclin F loss allows p130 to accumulate, whereas its overexpression promotes p130 degradation.
evidence: Based on experiments showing decreased p130 with cyclin F overexpression

claim: Cyclin F and p130 bind directly.
source: Cyclin F and p130 bind directly, and SCFcyclin F can ubiquitinate p130 in a fully reconstituted in vitro system.
evidence: Based on fluorescence polarization anisotropy assays and in vitro binding assays

claim: SCFcyclin F can ubiquitinate p130 in a fully reconstituted in vitro system.
source: Cyclin F and p130 bind directly, and SCFcyclin F can ubiquitinate p130 in a fully reconstituted in vitro system.
evidence: Based on in vitro ubiquitination assays using purified components

claim: A critical cyclin F binding motif in p130 is located at amino acids R680-L682.
source: We mapped a critical cyclin F binding motif in p130, and when that sequence is mutated, it prevents p130 ubiquitination and degradation.
evidence: Based on mutagenesis experiments showing that R680A L682A mutations prevent cyclin F binding and p130 degradation

claim: Mutation of the cyclin F binding motif in p130 prevents p130 ubiquitination and degradation.
source: We mapped a critical cyclin F binding motif in p130, and when that sequence is mutated, it prevents p130 ubiquitination and degradation.
evidence: Based on experiments showing that p130(AA) mutant cannot be ubiquitinated or degraded by cyclin F

claim: Expression of a mutant version of p130 which cannot be ubiquitinated accumulates in normal human fibroblast cells, causing slowed proliferation, an accumulation in G0/G1-phase, and apoptosis.
source: This mutant version of p130 accumulates in normal human fibroblast cells, causing slowed proliferation, an accumulation in G0/G1-phase, and apoptosis.
evidence: Based on proliferation assays, flow cytometry, and apoptosis assays in NHF-1 cells expressing p130(AA)

claim: Cyclin F contributes to inactivation of p130 and is a regulator of the CDK-RB network.
source: Taken together, our results suggest that cyclin F contributes to inactivation of p130 and is therefore a regulator of the CDK-RB network.
evidence: Based on multiple experiments showing cyclin F regulates p130 and correlation with CDK-RB network genes

claim: CCNF knockout is highly correlated with CDK4 and CCND1/Cyclin D1 knockout in the Cancer Dependency Map.
source: This finding is consistent with our observation that CCNF KO is correlated with CDK4 and CCND1/Cyclin D1 KO (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Based on Cancer Dependency Map data analysis

claim: Comparing Palbociclib to CRISPR knockout screens revealed CCND1/Cyclin D1 and CDK4 as the most highly correlated genes.
source: Comparing Palbociclib to CRISPR knockout screens, revealed CCND1/Cyclin D1 and CDK4 as the most highly correlated genes, validating this approach.
evidence: Based on Cancer Dependency Map drug sensitivity data analysis

claim: CCNF ranks ninth among over 17,000 genes queried for correlation with Palbociclib sensitivity.
source: Notably, CCNF ranked ninth among over 17,000 genes queried (Figure 8A).
evidence: Based on Cancer Dependency Map drug sensitivity data analysis

claim: For Ribociclib, CCND1 is the most highly correlated gene, CDK4 is ranked 5th, and CCNF is ranked 125th, falling within the top 1% of most highly correlated genes.
source: For Ribociclib, CCND1 is the most highly correlated, CDK4 is ranked 5th, and CCNF was 125th, falling within the top 1% of most highly correlated genes (Figure 8B).
evidence: Based on Cancer Dependency Map drug sensitivity data analysis

claim: Palbociclib and Ribociclib are among the top four most highly correlated drugs with CDK4 and CCND1 knockout.
source: Conversely, we determined which drugs are highly correlated with CDK4, CCND1, and CCNF KO. Palbociclib and Ribociclib are among the top four most highly correlated drugs with CDK4 and CCND1 (Figure 8C–D).
evidence: Based on Cancer Dependency Map drug sensitivity data analysis

claim: When CCNF/Cyclin F knockout is compared to all drugs tested, Palbociclib is ranked 1st, and Ribociclib is ranked 24th.
source: Remarkably, when CCNF/Cyclin F knockout is compared to all drugs tested, Palbociclib is ranked 1st, and Ribociclib is ranked 24th (Figure 8E).
evidence: Based on Cancer Dependency Map drug sensitivity data analysis

claim: CCNF knockout is highly correlated with both genetic and pharmacologic inactivation of the CDK-RB network across hundreds of cell lines.
source: Thus, CCNF KO is highly correlated with both genetic and pharmacologic inactivation of the CDK-RB network across hundreds of cell lines.
evidence: Based on Cancer Dependency Map data analysis showing correlations between CCNF knockout and CDK4/6 inhibitors

claim: As cells exit quiescence, p130 protein is degraded by the ubiquitin-proteasome system.
source: As cells exit quiescence, p130 protein is degraded by the ubiquitin-proteasome system.
evidence: Based on established knowledge about p130 regulation during cell cycle

claim: When cells transition from proliferation to quiescence, p130 protein levels significantly increase.
source: Then, when cells transition from proliferation to quiescence, p130 protein levels significantly increase (Smith et al., 1996).
evidence: Based on prior published studies

claim: The role of phosphorylation in controlling RB and the RB-like proteins has been well-established.
source: The role of phosphorylation in controlling RB and the RB-like proteins has been well-established (Canhoto et al., 2000; Farkas et al., 2002; Hansen et al., 2001); however, much less is known about how changes in the levels of RB-like proteins might contribute to changes in pathway activity or their ability to restrain E2F transcription factors.
evidence: Based on prior published studies

claim: As cells grow bigger, RB and its yeast ortholog Whi5 are diluted, contributing to cell cycle progression.
source: Notably, as cells grow bigger, RB and its yeast ortholog Whi5, are diluted, contributing to cell cycle progression (Schmoller et al., 2015; Zatulovskiy et al., 2020).
evidence: Based on prior published studies

claim: The targeted degradation of p130 by cyclin F, which rapidly reduces its concentration, plays a significant role in promoting cell cycle progression.
source: Our studies suggest that the targeted degradation of p130 by cyclin F, which rapidly reduces its concentration, also plays a significant role in promoting cell cycle progression.
evidence: Based on experimental results showing cyclin F regulates p130 degradation and affects cell cycle progression

claim: SCFSkp2 has been implicated in p130 degradation.
source: Skp2 has also been implicated in p130 degradation (Bhattacharya et al., 2003; Tedesco et al., 2002).
evidence: Based on prior published studies

claim: p130 has a different degradation pattern than p27.
source: However, p130 has a different degradation pattern than p27, and in a previous study, p130 was still degraded in Skp2 knockout cells (Tedesco et al., 2002).
evidence: Based on prior published studies

claim: p130 is still degraded in Skp2 knockout cells.
source: However, p130 has a different degradation pattern than p27, and in a previous study, p130 was still degraded in Skp2 knockout cells (Tedesco et al., 2002).
evidence: Based on prior published studies

claim: Skp2 overexpression had no effect on p130 levels in the experiments described in this manuscript.
source: Surprisingly, for unknown reasons, Skp2 overexpression had no effect on p130 levels in our experiments.
evidence: Based on experimental results showing no effect of Skp2 on p130

claim: Cyclin F has been linked to cell cycle gene transcription via its regulation of B-MYB, SLBP, E2F1, E2F2, E2F3a, E2F7, and E2F8.
source: Cyclin F has previously been linked to cell cycle gene transcription via its regulation of several proteins, including B-MYB, SLBP, E2F1, E2F2, E2F3a, E2F7, and E2F8 (Emanuele et al., 2020).
evidence: Based on prior published studies

claim: In response to DNA damage, cyclin F is able to bind to B-MYB and inhibit the ability of B-MYB to promote the expression of mitotic genes.
source: In response to DNA damage, cyclin F is able to bind to B-MYB, and rather than ubiquitinate it, inhibits the ability of B-MYB to promote the expression of mitotic genes (Klein et al., 2015).
evidence: Based on prior published studies

claim: In G2, cyclin F ubiquitinates the stem-loop binding protein (SLBP), which is required during S-phase to mediate histone biogenesis.
source: In G2, cyclin F ubiquitinates the stem-loop binding protein (SLBP), which is required during S-phase to mediate histone biogenesis (Dankert et al., 2016).
evidence: Based on prior published studies

claim: During G2, cyclin F catalyzes the ubiquitination of the activator E2Fs: E2F1, E2F2, and E2F3a.
source: Also, during G2, cyclin F catalyzes the ubiquitination of the activator E2Fs: E2F1, E2F2, and E2F3a (Burdova et al., 2019; Clijsters et al., 2019).
evidence: Based on prior published studies

claim: The ubiquitination of activator E2Fs allows for their degradation, and expression of mutant E2Fs that can no longer bind to cyclin F results in increased expression of E2F target genes.
source: The ubiquitination of activator E2Fs allows for their degradation, and expression of mutant E2Fs that can no longer bind to cyclin F results in increased expression of E2F target genes.
evidence: Based on established knowledge about E2F regulation by cyclin F

claim: During G2-phase, cyclin F regulates the atypical repressor E2Fs, E2F7, and E2F8, promoting their degradation.
source: Further, during G2-phase, cyclin F was shown to regulate the atypical repressor E2Fs, E2F7, and E2F8, promoting their degradation (Wasserman et al., 2020; Yuan et al., 2019).
evidence: Based on prior published studies

claim: Cyclin F regulates p130 degradation, and p130 regulates the expression of cyclin F, forming a double negative feedback loop.
source: Adding to the complexity of the role of cyclin F in cell cycle transcription, not only does cyclin F regulate p130 degradation, but p130 regulates the expression of cyclin F. Thus, cyclin F and p130 appear to exist in a double negative feedback loop, where each can downregulate the other.
evidence: Based on experimental results showing cyclin F degrades p130 and p130 is a DREAM target that represses cyclin F expression

claim: In response to DNA damage, cyclin F is downregulated by degradation.
source: Interestingly, in response to DNA damage, cyclin F is downregulated by degradation (D'Angiolella et al., 2012), and p130 has been suggested to become activated to repress cell cycle gene expression.
evidence: Based on prior published studies

claim: The degradation of cyclin F in response to genotoxic stress could preserve cell cycle arrest by allowing for the accumulation of p130.
source: Thus, the degradation of cyclin F in response to genotoxic stress could preserve cell cycle arrest by allowing for the accumulation of p130, while also contributing to increased nucleotide pools through the accumulation of another cyclin F substrate, RRM2 (D'Angiolella et al., 2012).
evidence: Based on experimental results and prior published studies

claim: In lung cancers, p130 expression negatively correlates with histological grading and metastasis.
source: In lung cancers, p130 expression negatively correlates with histological grading and metastasis ( Baldi and Esposito, 1997).
evidence: Based on prior published clinical studies

claim: For endometrial cancer patients who receive surgery, low p130 levels are significantly associated with increased recurrence and death.
source: For endometrial cancer patients who receive surgery, low p130 levels are significantly associated with increased recurrence and death (Susini et al., 1998).
evidence: Based on prior published clinical studies

claim: In vulvar carcinomas, loss of p130 and p27 contributes to carcinogenesis.
source: In vulvar carcinomas, loss of p130 and p27 has been shown to contribute to carcinogenesis (Zamparelli et al., 2001).
evidence: Based on prior published clinical studies

claim: In oral squamous cell carcinoma, p130-negative cases have worse prognoses than p130-positive cases.
source: In oral squamous cell carcinoma, p130-negative cases have worse prognoses than p130-positive cases (Tanaka et al., 2001).
evidence: Based on prior published clinical studies

claim: In thyroid neoplasms, reduced p130 expression has been linked to the aggressive characteristics of anaplastic carcinoma, while high p130 expression in micropapillary carcinoma has been linked to the smaller size of those tumors.
source: And, finally, in thyroid neoplasms, reduced p130 expression has been linked to the aggressive characteristics of anaplastic carcinoma, while high p130 expression in micropapillary carcinoma has been linked to the smaller size of those tumors (Ito et al., 2003).
evidence: Based on prior published clinical studies

claim: Cancers with low p130 expression or p130 loss grow more quickly and aggressively, whereas cancers with high p130 expression are correlated with better prognoses.
source: Thus, cancers with low p130 expression or p130 loss, seem to grow more quickly and aggressively, whereas cancers with high p130 expression are correlated with better prognoses.
evidence: Based on multiple prior published clinical studies

claim: p130 mRNA levels are not regulated during the cell cycle.
source: Since p130 mRNA levels are not regulated during the cell cycle, it is interesting to speculate that enhancing p130 degradation in some malignancies could contribute to defects in the regulation of cell cycle gene expression and hyper-proliferation.
evidence: Based on established knowledge about p130 mRNA regulation

claim: Enhancing p130 degradation in some malignancies could contribute to defects in the regulation of cell cycle gene expression and hyper-proliferation.
source: Since p130 mRNA levels are not regulated during the cell cycle, it is interesting to speculate that enhancing p130 degradation in some malignancies could contribute to defects in the regulation of cell cycle gene expression and hyper-proliferation.
evidence: Based on experimental results showing p130 degradation affects cell cycle gene expression

claim: Blocking p130 degradation could phenocopy CDK4/6 inactivation and could potentially be therapeutically advantageous.
source: Likewise, blocking p130 degradation could phenocopy CDK4/6 inactivation and could potentially be therapeutically advantageous, and would be consistent with our analysis showing that loss-of-function in cyclin D, CDK4, and cyclin F are highly correlated across nearly 800 cancer cell lines.
evidence: Based on experimental results and Cancer Dependency Map analysis

claim: Cyclin F is a strongly cell cycle-regulated gene with mRNA levels peaking in G2/M.
source: Cyclin F is a strongly cell cycle-regulated gene. Cyclin F mRNA levels peak in G2/M, and no studies have identified CCNF as an E2F target at G1/S.
evidence: Based on established knowledge about cyclin F expression

claim: No studies have identified CCNF as an E2F target at G1/S.
source: Cyclin F is a strongly cell cycle-regulated gene. Cyclin F mRNA levels peak in G2/M, and no studies have identified CCNF as an E2F target at G1/S.
evidence: Based on review of published literature

claim: AKT can phosphorylate and stabilize cyclin F, which could contribute to its accumulation near G1/S.
source: We previously showed that AKT can phosphorylate and stabilize cyclin F, and that this could contribute to its accumulation near G1/S (Choudhury et al., 2017).
evidence: Based on prior published studies

claim: The activation of cyclin F by AKT could potentially lead to the degradation of p130.
source: Thus, the activation of cyclin F by AKT could potentially lead to the degradation of p130.
evidence: Based on experimental results showing cyclin F degrades p130 and prior studies showing AKT activates cyclin F

claim: If cyclin F phosphorylation by AKT promotes p130 degradation, this would suggest that hyper-activated PI3K functions through cyclin F to render p130 inactive via the ubiquitin pathway.
source: Given the recurrent activation of the PI3K-AKT pathway in many cancers, it will be interesting in the future to determine if cyclin F phosphorylation promotes p130 degradation. If true, this would suggest that hyper-activated PI3K, either through mutation of PIK3CA or loss of PTEN, functions through cyclin F to render p130 inactive via the ubiquitin pathway.
evidence: Based on experimental results and established knowledge about PI3K-AKT pathway in cancer

claim: RB is phosphorylated by Cyclin-Dependent Kinases 4 and 6 (CDK4/6), as well as CDK2.
source: RB is phosphorylated by Cyclin-Dependent Kinases 4 and 6 (CDK4/6), as well as CDK2 (Narasimha et al., 2014; Rubin et al., 2020).
evidence: Based on prior published studies

claim: Phosphorylation of RB causes RB to dissociate from E2F, promoting the E2F-dependent expression of cell cycle genes that catalyze S-phase entry and cell cycle progression.
source: This phosphorylation causes RB to dissociate from E2F, promoting the E2F-dependent expression of cell cycle genes that catalyze S-phase entry and cell cycle progression (Rubin et al., 2020).
evidence: Based on prior published studies

claim: RB is a prototypical tumor suppressor due to its critical role in restricting proliferation.
source: Due to its critical role in restricting proliferation, RB is a prototypical tumor suppressor (Dyson, 2016).
evidence: Based on prior published studies

claim: p107 and p130 are tumor suppressors that prevent cell cycle gene expression by binding the repressor E2F proteins E2F4/5.
source: Both p107 and p130 are also tumor suppressors that prevent cell cycle gene expression by binding the repressor E2F proteins E2F4/5 (Claudio et al., 1994; Zhu et al., 1993), and both are also regulated by CDK-dependent phosphorylation (Canhoto et al., 2000; Farkas et al., 2002; Hansen et al., 2001).
evidence: Based on prior published studies

claim: p107 and p130 are regulated by CDK-dependent phosphorylation.
source: Both p107 and p130 are also tumor suppressors that prevent cell cycle gene expression by binding the repressor E2F proteins E2F4/5 (Claudio et al., 1994; Zhu et al., 1993), and both are also regulated by CDK-dependent phosphorylation (Canhoto et al., 2000; Farkas et al., 2002; Hansen et al., 2001).
evidence: Based on prior published studies

claim: p130 functions as part of the mammalian DREAM complex (DP, RB-like, E2F4/5, and MuvB).
source: Additionally, p130 functions as part of the mammalian DREAM complex (DP, RB-like, E2F4/5, and MuvB) (Litovchick et al., 2007; Smith et al., 1996).
evidence: Based on prior published studies

claim: DREAM assembles during quiescence and inhibits cell cycle progression by restricting the transcription of numerous cell cycle genes regulated by E2F, B-MYB, and FoxM1 transcription factors.
source: DREAM assembles during quiescence and inhibits cell cycle progression by restricting the transcription of numerous cell cycle genes regulated by E2F, B-MYB, and FoxM1 transcription factors (Fischer et al., 2016; Müller et al., 2012).
evidence: Based on prior published studies

claim: Perturbations to p130 or the DREAM complex allow expression of cell cycle target genes, shifting the balance from quiescence toward proliferation.
source: Accordingly, perturbations to p130 or the DREAM complex allow expression of its cell cycle target genes, shifting the balance from quiescence toward proliferation (Forristal et al., 2014; Iness et al., 2019; Patel et al., 2019).
evidence: Based on prior published studies

claim: In mice, Rb−/−p130−/− mouse embryo fibroblasts (MEFs) grow more rapidly in culture than MEFs deficient in either Rb or p130 alone.
source: In mice, Rb−/−p130−/− mouse embryo fibroblasts (MEFs) grow more rapidly in culture than MEFs deficient in either Rb or p130 alone, and Rb−/−p130−/− mice spontaneously form many more tumors than their respective single-gene knockouts (Dannenberg et al., 2004).
evidence: Based on prior published studies

claim: Rb−/−p130−/− mice spontaneously form many more tumors than their respective single-gene knockouts.
source: In mice, Rb−/−p130−/− mouse embryo fibroblasts (MEFs) grow more rapidly in culture than MEFs deficient in either Rb or p130 alone, and Rb−/−p130−/− mice spontaneously form many more tumors than their respective single-gene knockouts (Dannenberg et al., 2004).
evidence: Based on prior published studies

claim: In mouse models of small cell lung cancer, p130 knockout increases tumor size and overall tumor burden, even in the background of Rb and p53 loss.
source: In mouse models of small cell lung cancer, p130 knockout increases tumor size and overall tumor burden, even in the background of Rb and p53 loss (Ng et al., 2020; Schaffer et al., 2010).
evidence: Based on prior published studies

claim: p130 cooperates with RB to repress G2-M genes in response to genotoxic stress.
source: Consistent with its role as a tumor suppressor, p130 cooperates with RB to repress G2-M genes in response to genotoxic stress (Schade et al., 2019).
evidence: Based on prior published studies

claim: p130 loss in primary human fibroblasts leads to increased expression of cell cycle genes compared to loss of Rb alone.
source: And, p130 loss in primary human fibroblasts leads to increased expression of cell cycle genes compared to loss of Rb alone (Schade et al., 2020).
evidence: Based on prior published studies

claim: RB mutations, overexpression of cyclin D and cyclin E, loss of p130 protein, and dysregulation of the mammalian DREAM complex have all been implicated in increased cellular proliferation and tumorigenesis.
source: RB mutations, overexpression of cyclin D and cyclin E, loss of p130 protein, and dysregulation of the mammalian DREAM complex have all been implicated in increased cellular proliferation and tumorigenesis (Forristal et al., 2014).
evidence: Based on prior published studies

claim: p130 mutations are infrequent compared to other tumor suppressors like RB, CDKN2A, and p53, suggesting the possibility that post-translational mechanisms could account for its inactivation.
source: Interestingly, p130 mutations are infrequent compared to other tumor suppressors like RB, CDKN2A, and p53, suggesting the possibility that post-translational mechanisms could account for its inactivation.
evidence: Based on established knowledge about p130 mutations in cancer

claim: Cyclin F is a non-canonical cyclin that neither binds nor activates CDKs.
source: Cyclin F is a non-canonical cyclin—it neither binds nor activates CDKs (Bai et al., 1994; D'Angiolella et al., 2013).
evidence: Based on prior published studies

source: Instead, cyclin F is one of ~70 F-box proteins, a family of substrate recognition receptors that recruit substrates to the Skp1-Cul1-Fbox protein (SCF) E3 ligase (Bai et al., 1996; Cardozo and Pagano, 2004).

claim: SCF ligases play an evolutionarily conserved role in promoting cell cycle progression by triggering the destruction of cell cycle inhibitors.
source: SCF ligases play an evolutionarily conserved role in promoting cell cycle progression by triggering the destruction of cell cycle inhibitors.
evidence: Based on established knowledge about SCF ligases

claim: Yeast SCFCdc4 triggers the destruction of the CDK inhibitor Sic1.
source: For example, yeast SCFCdc4 and human SCFSkp2 trigger the destruction of CDK inhibitors Sic1 and p27, respectively (Carrano et al., 1999; Feldman et al., 1997; Schwob et al., 1994; Skowyra et al., 1997).
evidence: Based on prior published studies

claim: Human SCFSkp2 triggers the destruction of the CDK inhibitor p27.
source: For example, yeast SCFCdc4 and human SCFSkp2 trigger the destruction of CDK inhibitors Sic1 and p27, respectively (Carrano et al., 1999; Feldman et al., 1997; Schwob et al., 1994; Skowyra et al., 1997).
evidence: Based on prior published studies

claim: Cyclin F mRNA and protein levels oscillate during the cell cycle, giving cyclin F cell cycle-dependent activity.
source: Cyclin F mRNA and protein levels oscillate during the cell cycle, giving cyclin F cell cycle-dependent activity (Bai et al., 1994).
evidence: Based on prior published studies

claim: Cyclin F begins to accumulate at the G1/S transition, peaks in G2, and its protein levels are subsequently downregulated via proteasomal degradation in mitosis and G1.
source: Cyclin F begins to accumulate at the G1/S transition, peaks in G2, and its protein levels are subsequently downregulated via proteasomal degradation in mitosis and G1 (Choudhury et al., 2016; Mavrommati et al., 2018) where cyclin F is ubiquitinated by SCFβTRCP following cyclin F phosphorylation by casein kinase II (Mavrommati et al., 2018).
evidence: Based on prior published studies

claim: Cyclin F is ubiquitinated by SCFβTRCP following cyclin F phosphorylation by casein kinase II.
source: Cyclin F begins to accumulate at the G1/S transition, peaks in G2, and its protein levels are subsequently downregulated via proteasomal degradation in mitosis and G1 (Choudhury et al., 2016; Mavrommati et al., 2018) where cyclin F is ubiquitinated by SCFβTRCP following cyclin F phosphorylation by casein kinase II (Mavrommati et al., 2018).
evidence: Based on prior published studies

claim: Cyclin F is ubiquitinated by the cell cycle E3 Anaphase Promoting Complex/Cyclosome (APC/C).
source: Cyclin F is also ubiquitinated by the cell cycle E3 Anaphase Promoting Complex/Cyclosome (APC/C) (Choudhury et al., 2016).
evidence: Based on prior published studies

claim: Cyclin F has been implicated in the ubiquitination and degradation of several cell cycle proteins.
